meta.title: Developing a digital twin of MagAO-X for telemetry-based post-processing of high contrast imaging data
meta.authorsHtml: Matthijs Mars<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Louis Desdoigts<sup>1</sup>, Sebastiaan Haffert<sup>1,2</sup>

abstract: High-contrast imaging aims to detect faint companions and circumstellar material by suppressing on-axis stellar light, but residual structure in the stellar point spread function (PSF) still limits achievable contrast close to the star. Even with extreme adaptive optics, low-order aberrations and instrument/telescope vibrations can introduce time-variable leakage that is challenging to remove with post-processing methods that rely on diversity or reference observations. We present a telemetry-based forward-modelling approach that reconstructs low-order aberrations from a focal-plane low-order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS) and propagates them through a fully differentiable digital twin of the MagAO-X instrument to predict the stellar PSF. In simulation, we show that this approach can accurately model the stellar PSF and achieve post-processed images that are dominated by photon noise. We discuss a development path toward laboratory and onsky validation, and outline practical challenges such as telemetry data volume and the fusion of low- and high-order wavefront sensor estimates. These techniques can also be applied to space-based observatories like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO).

blocks.html: High contrast imaging aims to detect faint direct light from stellar companions or circumstellar disks. The challenge in directly imaging faint stellar companions stems from the often large difference in intensity of the sources as well as their close separation, causing the fainter signal of the companion to be hidden in the point spread function (PSF) of the orders of magnitude brighter star. In order to overcome this difference in intensity, high contrast imagers use a combination of coronagraphs to block on-axis stellar light, wavefront control to remove aberrations caused by atmospheric turbulence and optimise the wavefront for coronagraphic rejection, and post-processing techniques that attempt to remove residual stellar light in the images and thus reveal the faint objects of interest.

However, despite having extreme adaptive optics systems to deal with atmospheric aberrations, residual wavefront errors still persist after correction and additional aberrations can be added by vibrations of the instrument or telescope, reducing the coronagraphic performance and causing leakage of stellar light into the science images [1]. Current post-processing techniques often need specific observing strategies to be able to create a model of the stellar PSF that does not include the planet signal, which would cause self-subtraction of its signal. These observing strategies often include obtaining angular, spectral, or polarimetric diversity or observing reference stars. This usually constrains the instrument setup and observing strategy.

Telemetry-based forward modelling uses the information already gathered by the wavefront sensors during observation to reconstruct the residual wavefront aberrations and use this, combined with a detailed model of the instrument, to forward model the stellar PSF. This approach doesn’t model the PSF using the science images, avoiding the inclusion of planet signal in the stellar model. It also does not require any diversity or reference to create this model, but can be used in combination with current diversity-based observing strategies to improve its capabilities. The challenge for this approach is in creating an digital twin of the instrument that accurately recreates its response.

These digital twins are implemented in a differentiable framework, which makes it possible to calibrate them using gradient-based optimisation. This opens the door to hybrid physical–data-driven approaches in which most of the optical propagation is described by a physics model, while difficult-to-model effects (e.g. detector systematics) are captured by learned components. This approach combines the robustness of physics based modelling and the flexibility of data-driven methods. Similar differentiable models have been explored for space-based instruments, for example in the context of PSF calibration and exoplanet detection [2, 3]. Our work extends these ideas to a ground-based highcontrast imager and focuses on how such differentiable digital twins can be driven directly by telemetry for postprocessing. While we focus on a ground-based imager here, these techniques can be similarly applied to space based observatories, especially for telescopes like the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO).

In this paper, we present a forward modelling approach based on aberration reconstructions from a low-order wavefront sensor (LOWFS) using a digital twin of the MagAO-X instrument [4]. We demonstrate the feasibility in simulation by comparing the achieved contrast to that of having a photon-noise limited PSF model. Finally, we outline our approach implementing this for lab (and subsequently onsky) validation as well as discussing the challenges to be solved and the opportunities such techniques bring.

To demonstrate the technique of telemetry-based postprocessing we simulate a high contrast imaging instrument inspired by the MagAO-X instrument [4]. The MagAO-X instrument includes a pyramid wavefront sensor for primary wavefront sensing and AO control and the choice between two low-order wavefront sensors depending on the instrument setup. In this work, we focus on the focal plane low-order wavefront sensors (FLOWFS) that senses the on-axis light reflected off of a reflective focal plane mask. The particular coronagraph mask that we design for is a reflective lyot coronagraph with a diameter of 272µm (∼3λ/D in z-band). Figure 1 shows a schematic setup of our digital twin of the MagAO-X system consisting of two components; one model of the FLOWFS beam and one model for the science beam of the instrument. The FLOWFS model is calibrated to accurately match the instrument response in previous work [5]. For the science beam we simulate a simple system based on the MagAO-X design specifications and with its Lyot stop design. The model is fully differentiable allowing for calibration and reconstruction of wavefront aberrations using non-linear optimisation techniques.

Since the used reflective focal plane mask is only ∼ 3 λ/D in diameter, and because the contrast at small innerworking angles (IWAs) is limited mostly by low-order aberrations, we limit the aberrations of the wavefront to the first 9 Zernike modes (excluding piston, Noll indexing). Higher order aberrations are not considered in this feasibility demonstration, but will be part of future work and the upcoming laboratory demonstration.

We simulate monochromatic observations (λ = 908nm), corresponding to the central wavelength of MagAO-X’s z´filter. We generate 40000 frames of aberrated wavefront realisations of ∼30nm RMS, corresponding to 10 seconds of data gathered at 4kHz. The 9 random Zernike coefficients are drawn and normalised such that the generated wavefronts have an RMS that follows a Gaussian distribution with a mean of 30nm and standard deviation of 5nm and each of the modes has on average the same power. These aberrations are then forward modelled through both to the wavefront sensor and the science camera and simulate photon noise, with the photon counts representative for on-sky observations. We estimate the amount of photons using this formula:

With F0 ≈3·109 the approximate flux for a 6.5m telescope (such as the Magellan), T ≈0.3 the throughput efficiency, m the apparent magnitude and ∆t the exposure time. We simulate this for a 0th magnitude star with ∆t = 1/4000s to match the wavefront sensor framerate, resulting in 2·105 photons per wavefront sensor frame and 2·108 photons per science frame. The 1000 different realisations of the science camera images are added together to create 1 actual science frame. This setup is representative of the wavefront sensor imaging at 4kHz while the science camera is operating at 4Hz, typical for MagAO-X observing of bright targets in medium-good seeing conditions. For this setup we assume that the wavefront sensor and science camera are perfectly synchronised (with 1000 WFS frames corresponding to exactly 1 science frame). We don’t expect misalignment of a few frames to impact the performance of this approach significantly as it is averaged over many frames and also averages out when taking many science frames.

MagAO-X uses a reflective focal plane mask to measure low-order aberrations using the focal plane low-order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS). Using a digital twin of this FLOWFS system we reconstruct the aberrations of the incoming wavefront. Combining this with a digital twin of the science beam of the instrument in order to create a model of the stellar PSF. Subtraction of this model PSF from our science images removes stellar artefacts and reveals an injected planet in the post-processed image.

blocks.html: Since our digital twin is a fully differentiable optical model of the system, we can use non-linear optimisation in order to efficiently and accurately reconstruct the input aberrations from the wavefront sensor images. We minimise a correlation loss function comparing the observed (in this case simulated) wavefront sensor image with the forward modelled (during optimisation) image. The loss function is described as:

blocks.html: with xi the pixels of the forward modelled image x, and yi the pixels of the observed image y. Using the differentiability of our model, we can derive the gradient of this loss function with respect to the Zernike coefficients of the aberrations using back-propagation. The function is minimised using a L-BFGS-B optimiser in SciPy [6]. During reconstruction we first fit the tip/tilt coefficients followed by fitting all the input wavefront coefficients. Finally we do a final (short) optimisation using a MSE loss to fit the normalisation of the image. This final optimisation is necessary, because the used correlation loss is insensitive to flux scaling and can therefore not accurately fit this value.

The reconstructed wavefront aberrations are used to forward model the PSF for each of these realisations. The final model PSF for one science image is the sum of all the individual PSF frames as all those PSFs are seen during the span of one science frame. Additionally, we compute the true noiseless stellar PSF using the input aberrated wavefronts to act as our ground truth for comparison, subtracting this results in residuals that are photon-noise limited. The modelled PSFs are then subtracted from the science frame. This post-processing approach is also schematically shown in Figure 1 and can be performed for all science frames and subsequently combined with diversity-based observing strategies if wanted.

In Figure 2 we show the reconstruction of one of the wavefront aberrations from the simulated FLOWFS system. We can see that the response is recovered accurately and the residuals look mostly unstructured and noise dominated. When comparing the recovered aberrations to the true wavefront errors we recover mean reconstruction accuracy of 2nm RMS.

To demonstrate our approach we forward model these reconstructed wavefront aberrations using our digital twin to model the stellar PSF. Figure 3 shows the achieved 5σ contrast (the contrast needed to achieve a 5σ detection) as a function of separation. This is obtained by calculating the standard deviation of the post-processed residuals in 1 λ/D wide annuli around the centre of the star at varying separations. We compare the results of modelling the stellar PSF using our digital twin to using the ground truth PSF (purely photon noise limited) and the raw unprocessed contrast of our simulation. This curve is for 10 seconds of observation data with the science camera running at 4Hz and the FLOWFS running at 4kHz. We see that our reconstruction improves by order of magnitudes over using the unprocessed image, and performs similar to the ground truth model PSF, indicating that the final residuals are dominated by photon noise. All curves are normalised by the peak intensity of the stellar PSF without the Lyot coronagraph in the system, but including the Lyot stop to account for the throughput of the system.

blocks.caption: An example of a FLOWFS observation (left) and the reconstructed model image (centre) and the difference between those two (right). The model can fit the morphology of the observed PSF accurately and the residuals look mostly unstructured and dominated by noise, indicating a good reconstruction.
blocks.label: Figure

blocks.html: Additionally, we show a post-processed image with a 10−5 flux ratio injected companion at ∼2 λ/D separation. Using these 10 seconds of data, we recover this companion with an SNR of 70. The SNR is found by calculating the flux in a 1 λ/D annulus around the planet and compare this to the standard deviation of the noise in an 1 λ/D annulus around the star at the same separation as the planet. This post-processed image is filtered using a Gaussian filter with a FWHM of 1 λ/D to remove high-frequency residuals.

This feasibility study used a simplified, monochromatic, low-order simulation of the forward modelling postprocessing approach. The results show that telemetry-based forward modelling can provide stellar PSF models that approach the photon-noise limit, which could significantly improve our post-processing techniques. This particular approach based on aberrations measured by the low-order wavefront sensor is particularly useful at small IWAs where the leakage is dominated by low-order aberrations. Additionally, these techniques can be used in combination with existing diversity-based observing strategies to provide even better results.

In order to provide a more realistic demonstration of this technique, we are developing a realistic digital twin of the MagAO-X science beam using lab calibration data, which will include any non-common path aberrations in the system as well as higher order wavefront aberrations due to bench seeing. In order to accurately model the instrument response we are developing a hybrid digital twin that is mostly based on physics for the optical propagation. Though, effects that are more difficult to characterise will be learned using neural networks. To combine these physical and data-driven aspects of the model we are developing this digital twin using JAX, making it fully differentiable and allowing for easy optimisation of model parameters as well as integration of the data-driven layers. Our plan is to keep this digital twin mostly physical with data-driven components only for effects that can be difficult to physically describe or model (such as detector effects or (side-)effects introduced by the deformable mirror).

We are starting on a monochromatic model that works on narrow-band images and will work our way up to broadband modelling. Since our model will be mostly physical, this transition will only involve modelling any of the chromatic effects outside of the main optical propagation. Our first goal is to develop a digital twin that can model the instrument PSF accurately in laboratory conditions.

Some of the technical challenges that we still have to solve involve how to deal with the large amounts of data that will be created during an observation. Since our wavefront sensor is reading out at kHz speeds, a one hour observation typically leads to ∼30GB of just wavefront sensor data (32 × 32 pixel, 16-bit images at 4kHz). Additionally, we are also working on making a digital twin of the pyramid wavefront sensor in order to provide both high and low-order aberration estimates that we can use to forward model the PSF. However, how these two measurements can be combined for one PSF estimate is still an open question, considering their different frame-rates and overlap in sensitivity ranges.

We see that our forward modeled PSF perform as good as using the true noiseless PSF and thus give us residuals that are dominated by photon noise.
